column3: It explicitly joins prior reception with Muslim submission, closely echoing the queen's claim of prior knowledge and surrender.

God's opening of the breast to Islam gives a direct theological parallel to the queen's final submission.
Those given earlier scripture recognize the messenger through knowledge already available to them, closely matching prior knowledge enabling recognition.
Pharaoh's late claim to be among the Muslims contrasts with the queen's uncoerced and informed submission.
Joseph recognizes his brothers while they do not recognize him, a related case of asymmetrical recognition.
Joseph's brothers finally identify him after concealment and changed circumstances, closely paralleling recognition of an altered yet continuous identity.

Those given knowledge before the revelation recognize it on recitation, directly paralleling the focus's claim of prior knowledge before submission.
An appearance made to seem other than it is provides a close contrast to the queen's careful refusal to claim more than the visual evidence warrants.
God's naming of the community as Muslims before and in this revelation closely parallels the focus's retrospective Muslim self-description.
A deceiving appearance mistaken for water contrasts with the queen's cautious handling of what an altered object appears to be.
The command to be among the first Muslims directly supports the focus's language of submission.

Its people inwardly recognize God's signs but reject them arrogantly, forming a direct contrast to the queen's recognition that opens into submission.
